summary.title: Threat model of home
summary.description: A small home network used by a household of two adults, with laptops, phones and game consoles on the main network. Smart devices such as lights, a robot vacuum, cameras and a TV sit on a separate guest network, isolated from the main network. A Raspberry Pi on the main network provides DNS filtering with Pi-hole and a local recursive resolver with Unbound, and is managed over SSH with key login only. The model covers three zones: the main network, the internet and the guest network. Its purpose is to document threats and mitigations for a home lab as a learning and portfolio project. Out of scope are the internet provider’s own infrastructure and the vendors’ internal security.

threats.title: Hacked console used to reach other devices
threats.description: The console sits on the main network next to the laptops and the Pi. If it were taken over, it could be used to reach them.
threats.mitigation: Nintendo push regular security updates, installed automatically. Accepted on the main network for online and remote play.

threats.title: Hacked console used to reach other devices
threats.description: The console sits on the main network next to the laptops and the Pi. If it were taken over, it could be used to reach them.
threats.mitigation: Sony push regular security updates, installed automatically. Accepted on the main network for online and remote Play.

threats.title: Stolen MacBook gives access to accounts and the Pi
threats.description: One of the MacBooks holds the only SSH key to the Pi, the password manager and logged-in accounts. A thief could try to use them.
threats.mitigation: FileVault disk encryption on. Login password required.

threats.title: Malware on the MacBook uses the SSH key to reach the Pi
threats.description: If the MacBook got malware, it could use the saved SSH key to log into the Pi and change Pi-Hole or read the query log.
threats.mitigation: macOS updates installed. SSH key protected by a passphrase, also backed up in the password manager. The passphrase is saved in the Keychain, so it gives little protection while the Mac is logged in. Possible improvement: require approval for each use of the key.

threats.title: Lost or stolen iPhone gives access to accounts
threats.description: The iPhones hold the app accounts for the cameras, robot and lights, plus iCloud, photos and the password manager. A thief who unlocks the phone could use them.
threats.mitigation: Passcode and Face ID required. Find My on. Stolen Device Protection on.

cells.description: DNS filter, HaGeZi PRO + TIF blocklists

threats.mitigation: Strong unique password stored in the password manager. Dashboard accessed over HTTPS only. Only trusted devices on the main network; IoT devices isolated on the guest network.
threats.title: Unauthorised login to Pi-hole admin page
threats.description: Someone on the home network guesses or steals the admin password and logs into the Pi-hole dashboard.

threats.title: Blocklists or settings changed by an attacker
threats.mitigation: SSH with key only, strong admin password, HaGeZi lists from a trusted source.
threats.description: An attacker who gets into the Pi, through the admin page or SSH, could change Pi-hole's blocklists or settings. For example, they could allow a phishing site or send DNS lookups to a server they control, so family devices are directed to fake websites without anyone noticing.

threats.title: Query log reveals the family's browsing history
threats.mitigation: Log stored only on the Pi, admin page behind password and HTTPS, Pi reachable only from the main network
threats.description: Pi-hole's query log records every website name that the family's devices look up. Anyone who gains access to the Pi or the admin page could read it and see which sites each device has visited and when. The log stays on the Pi and is never sent outside the home

threats.title: Household loses internet when the Pi fails
threats.mitigation: Partly: backups exist and each device can switch DNS back. But the Pi is still a single point of failure.
threats.description: If the Pi stops working, for example because it is switched off, loses power, crashes or the microSD card fails, Pi-hole can no longer answer DNS lookups. All devices that use Pi-hole as their DNS server then cannot look up website names, so in practice they lose internet access.

threats.title: Changes to Pi-hole can't be traced to a person
threats.mitigation: Only one person has access to the admin account, so tracing isn't needed.
threats.description: Pi-hole's dashboard uses one shared admin password, not separate accounts per person. If a setting or blocklist is changed, it cannot be shown who made the change or when. In this household only one person administers the Pi, so the risk is accepted. In a business setting, individual logins and a change log would be needed.

cells.description: Every DNS lookup from the family's devices. Stored only on the Pi.
Key login only. Password and root login disabled.

threats.title: SSH access lost if the MacBook breaks
threats.description: The MacBook holds the only SSH key. If it is lost or broken, the Pi can't be reached over SSH.
threats.mitigation: Screen, keyboard and mouse connected directly to the Pi as a way back in. A new key can be added from there.

cells.description: Recursive resolver, DNSSEC, listens on 127.0.0.1:5335

threats.title: Pi-hole loses its upstream when Unbound fails
threats.description: If Unbound stops, or the ISP starts intercepting DNS traffic, Pi-hole has nowhere to send lookups, and websites stop loading.
threats.mitigation: Tested: the ISP doesn't intercept DNS, and sudo service unbound status shows whether it's running.

threats.title: Other devices use Unbound directly, skipping Pi-hole
threats.description: If Unbound answered other devices, they could skip the blocklists.
threats.mitigation: Unbound only listens on 127.0.0.1, so only the Pi itself can use it.

cells.description: Home Router. All traffic between the zones and the internet passes through it; those flows are left out to keep the diagram readable. Firewall Medium, UPnP on and not configurable, DMZ off, no port forwarding, behind CG-NAT. No traffic is allowed between the main network and the guest network (tested).

threats.title: Devices open ports without asking
threats.description: UPnP is on and can't be turned off in the router menu.  Any device on the network can open ports on the router without a password.
threats.mitigation: Behind CG-NAT, so opened ports can't be reached from the internet. Unknown rule found and removed. Checked with upnpc -l

threats.title: Router admin page taken over
threats.description: Someone who logs into the router admin page could change Wi-Fi, firewall or isolation settings for the whole home network.
threats.mitigation: Default admin password replaced with a strong unique one. Admin page not reachable from the guest network, tested.

threats.title: Account and play data stored by Nintendo
threats.description: Nintendo stores account details, purchases and play history, which the household doesn’t control.
threats.mitigation: Risk accepted. No payment card saved. Passkey and two-step verification on.

threats.title: Account and play data stored by Sony
threats.description: Sony stores account details, purchases and play history, which the household doesn’t control.
threats.mitigation: Risk accepted. No payment card saved. Login with passkey only.

cells.description: Photos, device backups, files

threats.title: Photos list with no independent copy
threats.description: Photos are synced between iCloud, the phone and the Mac, but there is no independent copy. A deletion or account lockout would affect all devices.
threats.mitigation: Planned: DIY NAS on the Pi with 3-2-1 backups. Keeping iCloud until a working backup exists.

threats.title: Robot data reveals when the home is empty
threats.description: The robot sends its map, cleaning times and status to Roborock's cloud. That data could show when nobody is home, and the household can't control how Roborock stores or protects it.
threats.mitigation: Risk accepted: the robot needs the cloud to work, and the floor plan itself is often public. Strong unique password on the Roborock account reduces the risk of someone else reading the data, but Roborock offers no two-factor login.

threats.title: Light data stored by Govee
threats.description: The lights send their status and schedules to Govee's cloud, which the household doesn't control. The data could hint at when someone is home.
threats.mitigation: Risk accepted: the lights need the cloud for app control, and the data is low value. Strong unique password on the account.

threats.title: Video stored or leaked by the cloud provider
threats.description: Live video and alerts pass through TP-link's servers, which the household does not control. No cloud recording and no microSD card, and alerts are text only, so no video or images are stored.
threats.mitigation: Accepted because the cameras need the cloud to work. Reduced risk by privacy mode when we're home. No cloud recording subscription and no microSD card, so video is not stored.

threats.title: TV sends viewing data to the manufacturer
threats.description: Smart TVs often send viewing habits and usage data to the manufacturer for advertising.
threats.mitigation: Advertising setting and partner consents turned off. Viewing information services off. Interest-based advertising off. Voice recognition off.

threats.title: Viewing habits stored by streaming services
threats.description: Streaming services store what the household watches and when.
threats.mitigation: Risk accepted. Normal for any streaming service, and the data is low value.

cells.description: External DNS servers run by independent organisations, outside the household’s control. Threats are covered on the flow from Unbound.

threats.description: The roborock may not get timely security updates. An attacker who takes over the robot could try to use it to reach other devices on the home network.
threats.title: Hacked roborock used to reach the main network
threats.mitigation: The roborock sits on "guest network", isolated from the main network. Isolation tested. Other devices on the guest network may still be reachable, not tested.

threats.title: Hacked light used to reach the main network
threats.description: The smart lights rarely get security updates. An attacker who takes over a light could try to use it to reach other devices on the home network.
threats.mitigation: The lights sit on "guest network", isolated from the main network. Other devices on "guest network" may still be reachable, not tested.

threats.title: Hacked camera used to attack other devices
threats.description: Cheap cameras rarely get security updates, so one could be taken over and used to reach other devices.
threats.mitigation: The cameras sit on "guest network", isolated from the main network.

threats.title: Hacked TV used to reach the main network
threats.description: Smart TVs rarely get security updates. An attacker who takes over the TV could try to use it to reach other devices on the home network.
threats.mitigation: The TV sits on the guest network, isolated from the main network. Isolation tested. The TVs remote support access is turned off.

threats.description: An attacker who gets the Roborock password, through a data leak or phishing, could log into the account from anywhere. They could control the robot and read its map and cleaning history.
threats.mitigation: Strong unique password stored in the password manager, replacing a reused one. Two-factor login not found in the Roborock app.

threats.title: Govee account taken over with stolen password
threats.description: An attacker who gets the Govee password, through a data leak or phishing, could log into the account from anywhere and control the lights.
threats.mitigation: Strong unique password stored in the password manager, replacing a reused one. Two-factor login not found in the Govee app. No API key created and no third-party accounts linked.

threats.description: Someone who gets the Tapo account password, through a leak or phishing, can log in from anywhere and watch the live video from inside the home.
threats.mitigation: A strong unique password and two-factor login.

threats.mitigation: Cleaning can be started and stopped with the buttons on the robot, without the internet or the cloud.

threats.mitigation: The lights can be switched on and off with the physical button on the lamp, without the internet or the cloud. Tested.

cells.description: Encrypted. Key login from the MacBook only.

threats.title: Unauthorised SSH login to the Pi
threats.description: An attacker who logs in over SSH gets full control of the Pi, including Pi-hole, Unbound and the query log.
threats.mitigation: Key login only from the MacBook, key protected by a passphrase. Password and root login disabled, tested.

cells.name: DNS lookups (DNSSEC)
cells.description: Two-way flow, drawn as one arrow for readability.

threats.title: Fake DNS answers sent to the family
threats.description: An attacker on the internet could send forged answers, so a website name points to a server they control.
threats.mitigation: Unbound checks DNSSEC signatures and rejects forged answers. But many domains aren't signed with DNSSEC at all, and for those, the check can't help. That's why it's only partly mitigated.

threats.title: DNS lookups visible to the internet provider
threats.description: Unbound asks the root and other DNS servers directly, but those lookups are unencrypted, so the ISP could see which sites are looked up.
threats.mitigation: Accepted, because it's still better than before: no single company gets the full list anymore.

cells.reasonOutOfScope: Set-top box not connected to any network. Wi-Fi setup failed because the remote can't type all the characters in the password.
